key:
1. Unsecured → tenor cap 60 months, max age 70, 18%/year → r = 1.5%/month. Adjusted tenor = min(60, 60, (70 − 35) × 12 = 420) = 60.  
2. PMT = 500,000,000 × 0.015 ÷ [1 − 1.015⁻⁶⁰] = 12,696,714.  
3. Character: current group 1, worst group 1, inquiries 2 (< 3; the 6-week-old inquiry is outside the one-month window), documents consistent → Clear.  
4. Purpose: invoice 900M = 400M own + 500M loan → Feasible.  
5. Collateral: N/A (Unsecured).  
6. Income: stated 38,000,000; verified (payroll) 36,000,000. Her husband's 41,000,000 is not counted (not a borrower). Existing (CIC) = 10,000,000.  
7. DTI = (10,000,000 + 12,696,714) ÷ 36,000,000 = 63.05% → ≤ 70% (Approve zone).  
8. Capital: liquid assets = 85M + 50M = 135M; reserve cover = 135M ÷ 22,696,714 = 5.95 months → Clear.  
9. Conditions: Favorable, Macro Normal → Normal.  
10. Precedence: no trigger → Approve.

Approve: Consequence: The 500,000,000 VND loan goes ahead as a plain approval, with no covenants attached. After paying her existing loan and the new installment, Phương Anh still has about 13 million VND a month (roughly 37% of her income) for the rest of her spending, and her liquid assets would cover close to six months of debt service if her income were ever interrupted.

Explanation: This is a clean Approve because every check comes back inside its line. Her income is a fixed monthly salary, confirmed by the employer's payroll file for twelve consecutive months, so it can be counted in full. The verified salary is 2 million lower than the one she stated, so the correct DTI is 63.05% rather than 59.7%. The decision is the same either way, but the figure is not, which is why income should always be checked against the Warehouse even when the verdict does not change.

The CIC record also needs careful reading. It shows two inquiries in the last month: this bank, and one other bank nine days ago for a car-loan quote. A third inquiry, from a card issuer, is six weeks old and falls outside the one-month window. Two inquiries are below the threshold, and the car-loan quote fits the purchase she is asking about, so there is nothing to investigate. If your DTI came out near 29%, you most likely added her husband's salary. He is not a borrower on this loan, so his income is not counted.

Key takeaway: Count only the verified income of the borrower, and count inquiries only inside the one-month window. A file in which no rule is triggered is a real answer too: the correct decision is then Approve.
Add conditions: Correct classification: Approve · Your choice: Add conditions

Consequence: Covenants and a recorded reason are attached to a file that has no risk signal behind them. A closer check for hidden debts would find nothing, because the CIC lists only her 10 million loan, so the extra process adds cost without telling the bank anything new.

Explanation: Add conditions is meant for files that carry a Watch or Adverse signal, such as a recent late payment, a thin cash buffer or a weak sector. This file has none of them. The most likely slip is on Character, where you may have counted three inquiries: this bank, the other bank nine days ago, and the card issuer. The card issuer's inquiry is six weeks old, so only two fall inside the last month.

The one-month window matters because several lenders asking about the same person at the same time can mean that the person is borrowing in many places at once, possibly with debts that are not yet on the CIC. Two inquiries, one of them explained by a car-loan quote, do not suggest that. The other two Cs are also clear: reserve cover is 5.95 months, well above the 3-month line, and the electronics manufacturing sector has a favorable outlook.
Key takeaway: The three-inquiry trigger applies to the last month only. Attach conditions when a rule is triggered, not as a precaution.
Reduce limit: Correct classification: Approve (DTI 63.05%) · Your choice: Reduce limit
Consequence: The amount is cut even though the full request fits within her repayment capacity. Phương Anh receives less than she needs for the SUV, and part of the credit room goes unused.

Explanation: Reduce limit applies only when DTI falls between 70% and 80%. A quick way to test it is to compute the maximum installment she could carry: 70% × 36,000,000 − 10,000,000 = 15,200,000 VND. That is higher than the requested installment of 12,696,714, so the full request already fits and there is nothing to cut. Her existing 10 million loan is already inside the 63.05%, so it should not be deducted a second time.

No single arithmetic slip pushes this file into the 70–80% range, so this choice usually comes from mindset. The loan looks large next to a 36 million salary, and it is tempting to trim it to be safe. The rules, however, judge the monthly burden, not the headline amount: a large loan only matters through the installment it produces.
Key takeaway: If the maximum installment is higher than the requested installment, the file is not a Reduce limit. Compare the installment with capacity before judging the size of the loan.
Reject: Correct classification: Approve (DTI 63.05%) · Your choice: Reject
Consequence: A borrower with clear repayment capacity is turned away, and 500 million of credit room goes unused when it could have supported a suitable case.
Explanation: DTI is 63.05%, about 17 points below the 80% reject line, and nothing else in the file reaches a Block. There are several mistakes that could have led you to Reject:

You may have counted household living costs as obligations. The family's spending of about 22 million VND a month is not debt repayment. Adding it would push DTI to about 124%, which is the tell-tale sign of this mistake.  
 You may have focused on the size of the loan (500 million) instead of the monthly burden. A large amount says nothing about repayment capacity until it is converted into an installment and compared with income.  
 You may have treated the unsecured loan type as a risk in itself. Loan type only selects the 18% rate and the 60-month cap, and both are already built into the 12,696,714 installment.
Key takeaway: Obligations in DTI are monthly debt repayments, not living costs, and a loan amount matters only through its installment.
Require more collateral: Correct classification: Approve · Your choice: Require more collateral

Consequence: The bank asks Phương Anh to pledge security for a loan that was never secured. There is no collateral to test, so there is no LTV, no shortfall and nothing to top up, and the request is delayed without any benefit to the bank.

Explanation: The loan is unsecured: she asks for it on the strength of her income, and she does not offer the apartment or the car. The collateral test therefore does not apply, and no LTV is calculated. The apartment appears in her dossier and in the Warehouse because she owns it jointly with her husband, but owning an asset does not make a loan secured. The loan type follows what is pledged to this loan, and here nothing is.

What the bank gets in exchange for taking no security is a different set of terms, not a collateral test: a higher interest rate (18% a year) and a shorter maximum tenor (60 months). Those terms are already inside the installment used to calculate DTI.
Key takeaway: Collateral is tested only when the loan type is Secured. An applicant's other assets do not turn an unsecured request into a secured one.

key:
1. Secured → tenor cap 360 months, max age 70, 11%/year → r = 0.9167%/month. Adjusted tenor = min(180, 360, (70 − 41) × 12 = 348) = 180.  
2. PMT = 700,000,000 × 0.0091667 ÷ [1 − 1.0091667⁻¹⁸⁰] = 7,956,179.  
3. Character: current 1, worst 1, inquiries 1, documents consistent → Clear. Purpose: 300M + 700M = 1,000M = deposit-agreement price → Feasible (near-miss: the sum matches but is not by itself the verdict). Acceptance: ownership Clear, transferable → Accepted.  
4. Income: stated 19,500,000; verified 19,500,000 (match). His wife's 7,000,000 is not his income (not a borrower). Existing (CIC) = 4,500,000 + 5,000,000 = 9,500,000 (he declared the car loan as 4,000,000).  
5. DTI = (9,500,000 + 7,956,179) ÷ 19,500,000 = 89.52% → > 80% → Reject. STOP.  
6. Steps 6–7 are not assessed (P-1, P-2). Noise only: LTV = 700M ÷ 1,060M = 66.0%; reserve cover = 60M ÷ 17,456,179 = 3.4 months; Industry Neutral. None of these changes the headline; the offer is None.

Reject: Consequence: The 700,000,000 VND loan does not proceed, and no credit room is used. If it had been approved, Kiên would have had only about 2 million VND a month of his salary left after paying his debts, against household spending of about 14 million a month, even allowing for the rent he would no longer pay.

Explanation: Several things in this file feel reassuring: six years with the same employer, a fixed salary, a clean CIC record (Group 1) and a house worth more than the loan. None of them changes what DTI measures, which is how much of the monthly income is already committed to debt. Here, existing debt of 9.5 million plus the new installment of 7.96 million adds up to 17.46 million, or 89.52% of his 19.5 million salary. Roughly 90 VND of every 100 VND he earns would go to debt service.

The difference between the car loan he declared (4.0 million) and the CIC figure (4.5 million) does not change the outcome: with the declared figure, DTI would still be 86.95%, which is still a Reject. It matters for another reason. It shows why declared debts must always be checked against the CIC, because a small understatement can combine with other misreadings and flip the decision. The core problem in this file is the debt he already carries, not only the size of the new loan.
Key takeaway: A file above 80% is rejected on the debt burden itself, before collateral or reserves are looked at. Declared debts must always be checked against the CIC.
Approve: Correct classification: Reject (DTI 89.52%) · Your choice: Approve

Consequence: A 700 million loan is made to a borrower who would spend almost 90% of his income on debt payments, and the approval also takes 700 million of credit room that could have supported a suitable case.
Explanation: There are several mistakes that could have led you to Approve:

You may have added his wife's income (7 million). This would give a DTI of about 65.87%. She is not a borrower on this loan, so she has no repayment obligation under it, and signing the mortgage consent as a co-owner of the house is not the same as co-borrowing. Her tailoring income also varies from month to month.  
 You may have combined that with the car loan he declared (4 million) instead of the CIC figure (4.5 million). On its own the declared figure still gives 86.95% (Reject), but together with his wife's income it drops DTI to about 63.99% and the decision flips.  
 You may have relied on the house and the 300 million of savings to justify approval. The house only makes the loan Secured, which selects the 11% rate and the 360-month cap. Its value plays no part in the DTI lines, and savings that are going into the purchase do not reduce his monthly debt burden.
Key takeaway: Count only the borrower's own income, and take existing debts from the CIC, not from the applicant's statement. Collateral and savings cannot make a debt burden affordable.
Reduce limit: Correct classification: Reject (DTI 89.52%) · Your choice: Reduce limit

Consequence: The file moves forward with a smaller loan, although the debt burden is already outside the zone in which a reduction applies. The bank would lend to someone whose existing debts already take nearly half of his income.

Explanation: Reduce limit and Reject answer different questions. Reduce limit asks whether the new loan alone is too large for the capacity that remains, so that a smaller loan could bring DTI back to 70%. Reject applies when the total debt burden is already too high. Here a maximum installment of 4,150,000 VND can be calculated (70% × 19,500,000 − 9,500,000), but above 80% the rule treats the burden as unsustainable and does not look for a smaller loan. His existing debts alone use about 49% of his income, so the problem does not lie in the size of the new loan.
If your own DTI landed between 70% and 80%, it is worth re-checking your work: you may have counted part of his wife's income or missed one of his CIC loans.
Key takeaway: Reduce limit fixes an oversized new loan, while Reject answers an unsustainable total debt.
Require more collateral: Correct classification: Reject (DTI 89.52%) · Your choice: Require more collateral

Consequence: The file is held while the bank asks for extra security that would not change anything. Repayment capacity, not collateral, is the problem, and the family would be asked for more assets for a loan they still could not service.

Explanation: Require more collateral comes into play only when DTI is 70% or below and the collateral is the weak point. Here the collateral is not weak at all: the house is appraised at 1,060,000,000 and carries no senior claim, so LTV on the 700 million loan is 66.0%, below the 70% maximum. Even if there had been a shortfall, extra collateral protects the lender after a default but does not make the monthly payments affordable.
Key takeaway: More collateral cannot fix a DTI above 80%. Capacity is tested first, and collateral only matters for a file that passes it.
Add conditions: Correct classification: Reject (DTI 89.52%) · Your choice: Add conditions

Consequence: Covenants are attached to a loan the borrower cannot service. Documents about the use of funds and periodic income updates would record the problem as it develops, but they would not prevent it.

Explanation: Add conditions is used for files whose DTI is at or below 70% and which carry a Watch or Adverse signal. This file has neither: DTI is far above the line, and Character is Clear (one inquiry, current and worst CIC group both 1). Covenants are checks made after disbursement. They never change the loan amount or the DTI, so they cannot turn an unsustainable debt burden into an acceptable one.
Key takeaway: Conditions follow an acceptable DTI. They do not rescue an unacceptable one.

key:
1. Unsecured → 60 months, max age 70, 18%/year → r = 1.5%/month. Adjusted tenor = min(60, 60, 312) = 60. PMT = 12,696,714.  
2. Character: current group 1 (the Group 2 label belongs to a late payment seven months ago, not to now); worst group in 12 months = 2 → Watch (history). Inquiries 1; documents consistent.  
3. Purpose: 400M + 500M = 900M = documented cost → Feasible. Acceptance: N/A (Unsecured).  
4. Income: stated 30,000,000 + 8,000,000 = 38,000,000. Verified (Warehouse): university six payroll lines 11,500,000 + 3,470,000 + 1,990,000 + 910,000 + 9,630,000 + 3,000,000 = 30,500,000; port-logistics job 8,000,000 + fixed responsibility allowance 2,000,000 = 10,000,000; total 40,500,000. Not counted: the 30M research payment (one-off), the brother's 3M (relative's support), her husband's salary. Existing (CIC) = 11,500,000 + card minimum 2,900,000 = 14,400,000; the card limit and balance are not monthly payments and the closed loan is not an obligation.  
5. DTI = (14,400,000 + 12,696,714) ÷ 40,500,000 = 66.91% → ≤ 70% (close to the line).  
6. LTV: N/A. Capital: L = 150M; reserve cover = 150M ÷ 27,096,714 = 5.5 months → Clear. Conditions: Neutral, Macro Normal → Normal.  
7. Precedence: Character Watch is the only trigger → Add conditions (reason recorded: Watch, 12-month history). Menu for an unsecured file: use of funds; income and occupation update.

Add conditions: Consequence: The loan is approved at 500,000,000 VND, with the reason recorded and covenants attached (for an unsecured file, the menu offers documents showing the use of funds and a periodic update of her occupation and income). The amount is not cut and Hạnh is not turned away, but the bank keeps a way to follow the file after disbursement.

Explanation: Her record is clean today, yet it shows a late payment within the last 12 months. A real bank does not ignore this: it records the reason and leaves the approving level to decide. In this simulation, that means the file can be approved only with conditions. This is what a Watch signal means. It is not a verdict on the applicant, but a flag that the file needs a closer look, and here the flag is raised by history, not by her situation today.

It is not a Block because a Block needs a debt that is overdue right now (current group 2 or worse) or signs of forged documents. A single late payment seven months ago on a loan she has paid on time ever since is history. It tells the bank that she slipped once, not that she is in default. It also does not change the numbers: DTI stays at 66.91%, reserve cover is 5.5 months and her sectors are neutral. The Watch signal changes how the loan is managed, not whether she can afford it. Your choice of covenants is feedback only and is not scored, because the rulebook does not prescribe which covenant fits which signal.
Key takeaway: A recent past delay is a Watch signal that attaches conditions. It does not change the DTI lines, and it is not a Block unless the debt is overdue now.
Approve: Correct classification: Add conditions · Your choice: Approve

Consequence: The loan is approved at the full amount, but the late payment within the last 12 months never reaches the approving level, and no covenants are attached. The bank has fewer ways to notice early if her repayment behavior or income changes.

Explanation: The numbers on this file are comfortable: DTI is 66.91% and reserve cover is 5.5 months. The signal is in the CIC record, which shows two different groups: the current group is 1, but the worst group in the last 12 months is 2. Reading only the current group misses the late payment, and Approve is reserved for files with no Watch or Adverse signal. If your DTI differed from 66.91% yet you still chose Approve, the decision may have been right for the wrong reason:

About 62.3% would mean you added her brother's monthly transfer, which is support from a relative and not income.  
 About 59.7% would mean you missed the credit card's minimum payment of 2.9 million.
Key takeaway: Approve is only for files with no Watch or Adverse signal, so read both the current group and the worst group in the last 12 months.
Reduce limit: Correct classification: Add conditions (DTI 66.91%) · Your choice: Reduce limit

Consequence: The amount is cut although her verified income and active debts show that she can carry the full 500 million. A lecturer with two stable incomes receives less than she needs for her child's studies.
Explanation: Two mistakes could have pushed your DTI into the 70–80% range:

You may have used the income she stated (38 million) instead of the verified income (40.5 million). This would give a DTI of about 71.31%.  
 You may have counted the closed consumer-finance loan (3.2 million a month). This would give a DTI of about 74.81%. The CIC shows a zero balance, so it is no longer an obligation.

With the correct figures, the maximum installment is 70% × 40,500,000 − 14,400,000 = 13,950,000 VND, above the requested 12,696,714, so there is nothing to cut. Because this file sits close to the 70% line, a small misreading is enough to cross it, which is why every figure needs to be read from the records.
Key takeaway: Use the verified income, which can be higher than the stated income, and count only debts that are still being repaid.
Reject: Correct classification: Add conditions (DTI 66.91%) · Your choice: Reject
Consequence: A lecturer with two stable incomes is turned away because of a misreading, and 500 million of credit room goes unused.
Explanation: There are several mistakes that could have led you to Reject:

You may have read the old Group 2 as a debt that is overdue now, which would be a Block. The CIC shows that her current group is 1. The group-2 episode was a 24-day delay about seven months ago, and she has paid on time since.  
 You may have counted only the university pay and forgotten the second job. This would give a DTI of about 88.84%. The Warehouse shows both employers paying every month.  
 You may have taken only the 11.5 million pay-grade salary and missed the other payroll lines. DTI would then exceed 100%. The allowances sit on their own lines, but they are all part of her monthly pay.  
 You may have used the card's balance or limit (58 million or 80 million) as a monthly obligation. Only the minimum payment of 2.9 million counts.

Key takeaway: A Block needs a debt that is overdue now or forged documents. An old label or a past delay does not block a file, and the CIC group is a prompt to read the record, not a basis for rejection.
Require more collateral: Correct classification: Add conditions · Your choice: Require more collateral
Consequence: The file is held for security that cannot be tested. Hạnh has not offered any asset, and she has said she does not want to pledge the family house.

Explanation: The loan is unsecured, so no collateral test applies and no shortfall can exist. The family house in the Warehouse (registered in her and her husband's names) is background information only, as it is not pledged to this loan. The Watch signal on Character leads to conditions on the loan, not to a request for security.
Key takeaway: Unsecured files cannot be a collateral shortfall, and a Character Watch is answered with conditions.

key:
1. Secured → 360 months, max age 70, 11%/year. Adjusted tenor = min(120, 360, (70 − 66) × 12 = 48) = 48 (the age cap binds).  
2. PMT = 450,000,000 × 0.0091667 ÷ [1 − 1.0091667⁻⁴⁸] = 11,630,485.  
3. Character: current 1, worst 1, inquiries 1; documents genuine and consistent (the gaps are in his statements, not in the documents) → Clear. Purpose: 300M + 450M = 750M = quote → Feasible. Acceptance: Accepted.  
4. Income: stated 8,000,000 + 24,000,000 + 15,000,000 = 47,000,000. Verified: pension 8,000,000 + shophouse rent 24,000,000 = 32,000,000. Rent arrives every three months (72,000,000 ÷ 3 = 24,000,000; 45,000,000 ÷ 3 = 15,000,000). Stability test on the evidence: the shophouse (same tenant for ten years, new registered five-year lease signed last month, rent paid into his account every quarter) is stable → counted; the let house (third lease at the address in four years, no extension registered, lease close to its end) is unstable → not counted; the renovated house has no tenant, not counted. Not income: deposits, the farmland sale, his wife's stall. Existing (CIC) = 8,000,000 + 4,500,000 = 12,500,000.  
5. DTI = (12,500,000 + 11,630,485) ÷ 32,000,000 = 75.41% → 70–80% → Reduce limit. Max installment = 70% × 32,000,000 − 12,500,000 = 9,900,000; max loan (PV, n = 48) = 383,045,069 ≈ 383,045,000. Grading tolerance ±5% on the installment: 9,405,000–10,395,000.  
6. LTV on the reduced amount: net collateral value 620,000,000 (no senior claim); LTV = 383,045,000 ÷ 620,000,000 = 61.8% → Clear. On the requested 450M the LTV would be 72.6%, above 70%, but the Reduce limit amount is the one assessed.  
7. Capital: 50M ÷ (12.5M + 9.9M) = 2.23 months → Watch both ways. Conditions: Neutral → Normal.  
8. Precedence: Reduce limit is the headline; Capital Watch is the secondary requirement (covenants: use of funds, collateral re-appraisal, income update).

Reduce limit: Consequence: The loan is adjusted from 450 million to about 383 million, a reduction of about 67 million. The new amount rests only on income that the verified records show to be stable. Covenants are attached because the couple's cash buffer is thin (reserve cover of about 2.2 months), and the collateral is Clear on the reduced amount.

Explanation: Four points are central to this file. First, the shophouse rent is stable. A tenant who has stayed for ten years and has just signed a new registered five-year lease gives a strong reason to expect the rent to continue throughout the loan. Second, the rent from the other house is not stable. It is the third lease at that address in four years, no extension is registered and the lease is close to ending, so there is little evidence that this tenant will stay. The renovated house has no tenant, so it earns nothing yet. Third, his age shortens the tenor from 120 to 48 months, which raises the installment to 11.6 million and is the reason his DTI is higher than a 120-month schedule would suggest. Fourth, the Capital Watch is a secondary requirement. It does not change the amount or the DTI, but it is the reason covenants are attached on top of the reduction.
Check on the amount you entered:

Within the accepted range (9,405,000–10,395,000 VND): You counted the pension and the shophouse rent, deducted both of his active debts and applied the 70% line. The system converts your figure into a loan amount over the 48-month tenor.  
 Below the range: The rule asks for the maximum installment that brings DTI back to exactly 70%, so a lower figure leaves part of his capacity unused. Possible reasons: only the shophouse rent was counted (about 4.3 million); quarterly rent was divided by 4 instead of 3 (about 5.7 million); one debt was deducted twice; the 3 million of school fees was deducted as if it were debt (about 6.9 million); or 60% was used instead of 70% (about 6.7 million).  
 Above the range (a loan of about 402 to 450 million): A figure above the range is still below the requested installment, so the system accepts it, but it does not bring DTI back to 70%. Possible reasons: a percentage above 70% was used; his current DTI of 75.4% was used as the target, which leaves the loan almost unreduced; his debts were read as 11.5 million instead of 12.5 million (giving 10.9 million); or part of the unstable rent was counted.

Key takeaway: Judge each income stream on the evidence of how stable it is, such as the length of the tenancy, whether the lease has been renewed, and who is paying and how, and count only the streams that pass. Rent paid quarterly must also be converted to a monthly figure.
Approve: Correct classification: Reduce limit (DTI 75.41%) · Your choice: Approve

Consequence: The 450 million loan is approved on the assumption that the rent from the second house will keep coming in, although its tenancy has changed three times in four years and no extension is registered. If that rent stops, his income falls to the pension plus the shophouse rent, and the full installment becomes hard to afford. The approval also takes about 67 million more credit room than the correct answer.
Explanation: There are several mistakes that could have led you to Approve:

You may have used the income he stated (47 million), or counted the 15 million rent as stable. Both give a DTI of about 51.3%. That rent comes from a tenancy that has changed repeatedly and has no registered extension, so it cannot be relied on.  
 You may have counted the 12 million advertised rent of the renovated house. This would give a DTI of about 54.8%. That house has no tenant, and income that has not yet been received cannot be counted.  
 You may have read the quarterly rent as monthly (72 + 45 million). This would give a DTI of about 19.3%. Quarterly payments must be divided by 3.  
 You may have missed the 4.5 million personal loan in the CIC. This would give a DTI of about 61.3%.

Key takeaway: Income counts only when the evidence shows that it will keep arriving. A long tenancy and a newly registered long lease support stability, while frequent tenant changes, a lease near its end without renewal, or no tenant at all do not.
Reject: Correct classification: Reduce limit (DTI 75.41%) · Your choice: Reject
Consequence: A borrower with 32 million of reliable monthly income is rejected instead of being offered a loan of the right size, and about 383 million of credit room goes unused.
Explanation: There are several mistakes that could have led you to Reject:

You may have decided that the shophouse rent was too uncertain to count, for example because you doubted that it would last as long as the loan. The evidence says the opposite: the same tenant has rented it for ten years and has just signed a new registered five-year lease. Excluding it leaves only the 8 million pension and a DTI above 300%.  
 You may have treated his age (66) as a reason to reject. Age only shortens the tenor, up to age 70, which raises the installment. It is not a ground for rejection.  
 You may have counted the tenants' deposits (78 million) as a monthly obligation. They are sums to be returned when the leases end, not monthly payments.  
 You may have decided that rental income in general is unreliable and excluded all of it. Each rental stream should be judged on its own evidence.

Key takeaway: When part of an applicant's income is unreliable, exclude only that part and calculate DTI on the income that remains. Rejecting the whole file would ignore the stable income the applicant demonstrably has.
Require more collateral: Correct classification: Reduce limit (DTI 75.41%) · Your choice: Require more collateral

Consequence: The file is held for extra security although the security is not the problem. The couple are asked to pledge more assets for a loan whose real issue is that the installment is too large for their income.

Explanation: Require more collateral applies only when DTI is 70% or below. The mistake is understandable, because the numbers on the collateral side are close to the line: the house is appraised at 620 million, so LTV would be 72.6% on the full 450 million, above the 70% maximum. But the file first fails the capacity test, and the amount that survives that test is the reduced 383 million. On that amount LTV is 61.8%, so no shortfall remains. The 8 million loan is also not a senior claim on this house, because it is secured on the renovated third house.
Key takeaway: Capacity is decided first, and collateral is checked on the amount that survives it.
Add conditions: Correct classification: Reduce limit (DTI 75.41%) · Your choice: Add conditions
Consequence: The full 450 million is approved with covenants, although DTI is above the approval line. The covenants record the risk but do not reduce the installment he would have to pay.

Explanation: Add conditions needs DTI of 70% or below. The Capital Watch is real: the couple's savings of about 50 million cover only about 2.2 months of debt service, below the 3-month line. However, it appears as a secondary requirement on the Reduce limit decision. It adds covenants to the reduced loan but does not replace the reduction, because covenants never change the loan amount or the DTI.
Key takeaway: A lower-order signal never outranks a DTI above 70%. Reduce the loan first, then attach conditions to what remains.

key:
1. Secured → 360 months, max age 70, 11%/year. Adjusted tenor = min(240, 360, 372) = 240. PMT = 680,000,000 × 0.0091667 ÷ [1 − 1.0091667⁻²⁴⁰] = 7,018,881.  
2. Character: current group 1 (the Group 2 was a payment four months ago, now regularised); worst group in 12 months = 2 → Watch (history). Inquiries 1. Purpose: 320M + 680M = 1,000M = price → Feasible. Acceptance: Accepted.  
3. Income: stated "around 45,000,000" (15,000,000 + about 30,000,000). Verified: editor's salary 15,000,000. The 335,000,000 of advertising over 12 months (average about 27,900,000) is paid per campaign, with seven empty months and no contract beyond each campaign; the three negotiated campaigns have no contract; the 18,000,000 insurance payment is one-off. Explanation: The central question in this file is which part of his income can be relied on every month. The editor's salary arrives in the same amount every month under a permanent contract, so it counts. His advertising income can be large in a good month, but it is not regular: each payment comes from a separate campaign contract with a different advertiser, seven of the last twelve months had no payment at all, and no contract continues beyond its own campaign. The monthly average of about 27.9 million in the records is the most misleading figure in the file, because it describes a total spread over twelve months and not something he can expect to receive each month. The three campaigns under negotiation have no signed contract, so they are not income yet.

His existing debt is also higher than he declared: 4.2 million, or 28% of his salary, against the 2 million he stated. On the 15 million salary, DTI is 74.79%, which places the file in the Reduce limit zone. The late payment four months ago does not change that. It is a Watch signal about history, which adds covenants to the reduced loan but does not replace the reduction.
Check on the amount you entered:

Within the accepted range (5,985,000–6,615,000 VND): You calculated on the 15 million salary alone, deducted both of his active CIC loans and applied the 70% line. The system converts your figure into a loan amount over the 240-month tenor.  
 Below the range: The rule asks for the maximum installment that brings DTI back to exactly 70%, so a lower figure leaves part of his capacity unused. Possible reasons: a debt was counted twice, for example both the 2 million he declared and the 2.8 million in the CIC, together with the 1.4 million plan (about 4.3 million); living costs were deducted as if they were debt, such as the 1.5 million of after-school classes (about 4.8 million) or the rent (a figure near zero); 60% was used instead of 70% (about 4.8 million); or an extra cushion was added for the advertising risk, which had already been excluded and is therefore counted twice.  
 Above the range (a loan of about 641 to 680 million): A figure above the range is still below the requested installment, so the system accepts it, but it does not bring DTI back to 70%. Possible reasons: a percentage above 70% was used; his current DTI of 74.8% was used as the target, which leaves the loan almost unreduced; his debts were understated by about 0.35 to 0.7 million; or some advertising income was added to the salary.

Key takeaway: An average of irregular payments does not describe what the applicant will actually receive each month, so it should not be treated as income. Count the income that arrives regularly, calculate DTI on that amount, and then compare the result with the 70% and 80% lines.

Consequence: The 680 million loan goes ahead on income that may not recur. If the advertising payments stop, his 15 million salary has to cover 4.2 million of existing debt plus a 7.0 million installment, which leaves only about 3.8 million a month for everything else. The approval also takes about 70 million more credit room than the correct answer.
Explanation: There are several mistakes that could have led you to Approve:

You may have used the income he stated (45 million). This would give a DTI of about 24.9%. That figure includes advertising income that the verified records do not support as a regular monthly receipt.  
 You may have added the average advertising income (27.9 million) to his salary. This would give a DTI of about 26.2%. The records show that each campaign is a separate contract, and that seven of the twelve months had no payment.  
 You may have used only the debt he declared (2 million). This would give a DTI of about 60.1%. The CIC shows 2.8 million for the personal loan.  
 You may have used the CIC personal loan (2.8 million) but missed the equipment installment plan. This would give a DTI of about 65.5%. Both active loans count.

Key takeaway: Income that varies from month to month and is not secured by a contract should not be included in DTI, even when the amounts are large. Large payments in some months do not show what he can pay every month.

 You may have counted living costs as obligations. Adding the 12 million rent alone pushes DTI above 150%. Only debt repayments count.

Require more collateral: Consequence: The loan can proceed at 1,000,000,000 VND if about 169 million of extra collateral is pledged. Covenants are attached because of the three inquiries and the sector outlook. The borrower can afford the payments, but the lender's cushion is too thin on the plot as it stands.

Explanation: The plot looks worth 1.96 billion, but another lender is paid first from it. Bank X holds a first-ranking mortgage of 700 million, and the new loan would rank second, so only 1.26 billion of the plot's value actually stands behind it. A 1 billion loan against 1.26 billion gives an LTV of 79.37%. If the plot had to be sold at its appraised value, the bank would be repaid but with a cushion of about 21%, compared with the 30% implied by the 70% maximum.

There are two ways to cure the gap. The first is a smaller loan: 70% × 1,260,000,000 = 882,000,000. The second is more collateral: 1,000,000,000 ÷ 0.70 − 1,260,000,000 = 168,571,429, which the system rounds up to 169,000,000. Note that the extra collateral is not simply the 118 million by which the loan exceeds 882 million. Collateral worth 118 million would only support 70% of that amount in lending, so it must be divided by 0.70, which gives exactly the same 168.6 million.

Check on the amount you entered: your figure is graded within ±5% of the system's 169,000,000 (160,550,000–177,450,000). A figure near 118 million means you subtracted 882 million from the loan and forgot to divide by 70%. A zero or negative figure means the senior claim was ignored, because 1,000,000,000 ÷ 0.70 is then smaller than the full 1.96 billion appraisal.
Key takeaway: Net collateral value is the appraised value minus the claims that rank ahead of the new loan.

Consequence: One billion is lent against a plot whose free value covers only 882 million at the 70% line. If the plot has to be sold, Bank X is paid its 700 million first, and any fall in price below the appraisal lands on the new lender. The approval also uses 1 billion of credit room without the gap being cured.

Explanation: Ignoring Bank X's claim gives an LTV of 51.0%, which looks comfortable and is the tell-tale sign of this mistake. The claim ranks ahead of the new loan, so it has to be deducted before LTV is calculated. The file also carries three inquiries in one month and an unfavorable main income source. Those signals would have attached covenants even on an approval, so the approval would have been incomplete as well as unsafe.
Key takeaway: Always net the senior claims off the appraised value before computing LTV.

Consequence: Covenants are attached, but the collateral gap stays open. The bank would hold a second-ranking claim that covers only part of the loan with the required cushion, and the covenants do not add to that cover.

Covenants are checks made after disbursement, such as documents on the use of funds or a periodic re-appraisal of the plot. They do not change the loan amount or the LTV.
Key takeaway: Require more collateral comes before Add conditions in the decision order, and covenants never repair a shortfall.

Consequence: The amount is cut on a ground that does not exist. His income can carry the full installment, so a capacity-based reduction would give up lending that the numbers support.

Explanation: Reduce limit needs DTI above 70%. Here DTI is 48.11%, or 27.2% if the Bank X installment was missed. Both are far below the line. The 882 million figure looks like a reduced loan, but it comes from a different test: it is the largest loan the collateral supports at the 70% maximum LTV, and it is one of two ways to cure the shortfall. The two decisions may produce similar-looking amounts, but they answer different questions.
Key takeaway: Reduce limit answers whether he can afford the payments, while Require more collateral answers whether the lender is covered.

A matching amount shows only that the paperwork adds up, not that it supports the stated purpose. The distinction matters because the repayment source changes. The bank assessed an engineer's salary for a home improvement, but a new business would carry its own risk of failure on top of his debts. The bank has no view of that business, so it cannot judge whether the loan can be repaid.
Key takeaway: Documents must support the stated purpose, not merely the amount.
